extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing USPTO guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility framework: identifying whether additional claim elements amount to an "inventive concept" (i.e., significantly more than a judicial exception) by evaluating elements individually and in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: identify and evaluate additional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s). Examiners should identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate additional elements with respect to Supreme Court-identified considerations discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or every claim. The evaluation is not a weighing test; it is important to assess the significance of additional elements relative to the invention and whether they encompass an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry-over from Step 2A Prong Two and re-evaluation of 'insignificant extra-solution activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should carry over their identification of additional elements and conclusions from Step 2A Prong Two on considerations discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(c),(e),(f),(h). Elements previously considered 'insignificant extra-solution activity' should be re-evaluated in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-evaluation finds that an element is unconventional or otherwise more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity, that finding may indicate the element is no longer insignificant. Also evaluate whether additional elements merely append well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality per MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome determination at Step 2B (Pathway C eligibility vs ineligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole does amount to significantly more than the exception (there is an inventive concept), the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete. If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more (no inventive concept), the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine each claim for eligibility separately; similar claims in the same application should not automatically be judged to stand or fall together. For example, a dependent claim may be eligible even if the independent claim is not. See MPEP § 2106.07 for how to formulate an ineligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to functioning of a computer or other technology (improvement consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field (i.e., whether it provides a technological solution to a technological problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improvement to conventional computer functioning or other technology is asserted, the specification should provide a technical explanation sufficient for one of ordinary skill in the art to recognize the claimed invention as providing the improvement. Conclusory assertions in the specification are insufficient. An indication of improvement can include identification of a technical problem and details of an unconventional technical solution or identification of technical improvements over the prior art. After consulting the specification, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect disclosed improvement and be evaluated as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must include the components or steps that provide the improvement described in the specification (though it need not explicitly state the improvement). The claim should be evaluated "as a whole" as an ordered combination without ignoring individual step requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to determine if the claim reflects an improvement. Avoid oversimplifying claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for specific claim requirements. Improvements may be provided by one or more additional elements alone or in combination with the judicial exception (see Diamond v. Diehr and Finjan discussions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and admissible evidence when examiner finds no improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner concludes the disclosed invention does not improve technology, the burden shifts to the applicant to provide persuasive arguments and any necessary evidence to demonstrate that one of ordinary skill in the art would understand the disclosed invention as improving technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 (e.g., declarations) must establish what the specification would convey to one of ordinary skill and cannot be used to supplement the specification. See MPEP § 716.09 and § 1.132 practice for declarations responding to 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-functionality criterion: improves computer capabilities vs using computer as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-related inventions, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (improvement in computer functionality) or merely uses computers as a tool to implement an abstract idea or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases where courts found improvements in computer functionality include specific data structures that change how data is stored/retrieved (Enfish), inventive distribution of network functionality (Bascom), particular ways of programming or structuring software, particular memory systems, technical details for transmission or image processing, improved user interfaces, and similar concrete technical solutions. The specification's disclosure of how to implement the improvement is important (technical details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation to computer implementation and mental-process exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A method claim must be limited to computer implementation (under the BRI) in order to be an improvement to computer functionality; if the entire scope can be performed mentally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that cover embodiments performable without a computer (e.g., verbally or by phone) or that can be performed mentally fail the improvement-in-computer-functionality criterion (Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; RecogniCorp v. Nintendo). Ensure the claim scope is not purely mental or performable without computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns: examples insufficient to show computer-functionality improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain kinds of claim features have been held insufficient to demonstrate an improvement in computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples courts have indicated may not be sufficient include: functionally claimed restaurant menus (Ameranth); speedups that arise solely from using a general-purpose computer (FairWarning); mere automation of manual processes using generic computers (Credit Acceptance, LendingTree non-precedential); recording/transmitting/archiving digital images with conventional tech absent technical details (TLI Communications); affixing a barcode without technical details (Secured Mail Solutions); instructions to display information without specifying how to achieve it (Interval Licensing); improving stored information rather than database functionality (BSG Tech); arranging GUI information to help humans process faster (Trading Technologies). Use these as anti-pattern guidance when assessing claimed improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to other technologies or technical fields (non-computer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in technology beyond computer functionality may establish eligibility; the improvement must be a technological improvement, not merely an improvement in an abstract idea or business practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found eligibility for improvements in fields such as preservation processes in life sciences (Rapid Litigation Management v. CellzDirect), particular computerized control of machinery (Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), improved content downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs), improved data compression (DDR Holdings), virus screening methods (Symantec), and components or techniques that generate new data (Electric Power Group). An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., a better economic concept) is not an improvement in technology (Trading Technologies).
